Philippolis - A place to catch your breath

By: Diana Lucas | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
In the 1960's the great Karoo through road was built, the N1 highway establishing what was to become a popular road trip between Johannesburg and Cape Town. But the highway bypassed the small town of Philippolis and there was great sadness amongst its residents. No tourist trap, no motels, or immediate job bonanza for the locals. The three petrol stations that the town boasted dwindled to one. Buildings and farms were abandoned as residents left for more lucrative locations.

But the N1 omission has turned out to be a blessing in disguise. This little southern Free State dorp tucked away off the N1 at the toe of the Horizon Route has the idyllic atmosphere you would expect of a Karoo town and has retained its old world charm mingled with an air of benevolent neglect.

The London Missionary Society founded Philippolis in 1823 as a mission station to serve the local Griquas. This makes it the oldest settlement town in the Free State at over 200 years.

Philippolis has retained most of its Karoo architecture. Wide streets, slope-roofed homes, the Dutch Reformed Church (which centres the town) has an imposing organ gifted by the Jewish Community (more of this later) to the Boers after the Anglo Boer War.



Further information:
Nicolene Gibbons, an international pianist (of some repute) bought a small 32 square metre place in the town and while she lectures at Free State University in the week, on the weekends she's in 'Philly' playing the organ at Sunday's church service.

This was the home of Sir Laurens van der Post ( his ashes are in the Memorial Garden and the museum has some of his original works) and Griqua leader Adam Kok. Human rights activist Emily Hobhouse established a weaving and spinning school in 1905 for the destitute. More contemporary, this is Brumilda Van Rensburg's home town and Banyana Banyana striker Nthabiseng Majiya ( remarkable that she made the team if you see the condition of the local soccer field)

The town played a central role in the Anglo Boer war. Captured by the British, Philippolis came under siege in 1900 during the Boer Commando's struggle to liberate it. Raids and skirmishes between the two sides during this time created a huge occupancy of the local jail house. Today the jail has occupants of a different kind, it's been transformed into an overnight stay for tourists. A more traditional way to experience the history is with historian and journalist Doreen Atkinson. Doreen has vivid stories to tell and she is committed to telling the history of the area reaching out to other museums in the area.

Meintjies Louw - Head of the Griekwa community in town, will talk about their history and heritage.

Being so close to Joburg, Philly has become a popular semigration spot... Hanneke and her husband Kevin (an editor on international documentaries which is slightly problematic with the sometimes shaky internet connections ) moved here from the City of Gold. They bought a vacant lot of land and have planted vines, experimenting with farming on bio dynamic principles and natural fermentation. The first harvest will be next year but this week she has an experimental first 40 litres to taste. Haneke has also restored some of the old homes where tourists can stay.

Another new resident with as story to tell is Neil Underhay - Neil moved with his two children a year and a half ago. A carpenter he made bespoke furniture in Joburg. He bought a half acre plot and started bee keeping…bees and the study of bees had become more and more of his passion. Only beekeeper in this area.. He started to make mead…using not just the honey but the honey comb all parts of the hive. Neil has recently become head of the Free State SAMMA (South African Mead Masters Association) chapter.

Philippolis has always attracted eccentric and interesting characters like salesman Jacob Novozenitz, from Lithuania, at the turn of the 20th century. Local Boer farmers gave him money to bring out the rest of his family and this was the beginning of the Boere-Jode in the dorp (and the organ which was donated to the NG Kerk in gratitude). Because the Boers could not pronounce Novozenitz, the was known as Jacob 'Jacob' which eventually transformed to Jacobson.

'Queen of the Free State 'and 'The Messiah's Dream Machine' by author Jennifer Friedman (originally Jacobson) are two memoirs of her childhood and her eccentric family – the Jacobsons. The 'dream machine', a series 1 Land Rover, can be found in brothers Wilfred and Benjamin Jacobson's farm. They farm sheep, produce wool. And continue the Jacobson's legacy of eccentricity.

Script:


(Claire) In the 1970’s the Great Karoo through road, the N1 was built. This would become the popular road trip between Johannesburg and Cape Town. But it bypassed the small town of Philippolis which was great sadness to the town because it would mean, no tourists traps, no petrol stations no hotels…… But on reflection the N1 omission was a blessing in disguise.

(Claire) At over two hundred years old it’s the oldest settlement town in the Free State and on a freezing winter’s morning you can easily imagine a bygone time the streets are empty, and you can feel the quiet.

(Doreen) It's the atmosphere. It's a old world atmosphere. The houses, the architecture, the quietness, the open streets.

(Claire) Doreen Atkinson is an historian who made this dorp her home in 1994 when she and her husband were on a road trip. It was love at first sight.

(Doreen) I went for a walk that morning. I found the house with a tiny little sign in the window saying for sale. And, I went back to my husband, who was at the hotel, and I said to him, I found us a house.

(Claire) You just came for a holiday?

(Doreen) Ya we just drove through. We thought this is super special, this is a Victorian old lady. It's a gem.

(Claire) Built in 1874, this was the home of Sir Laurens Van de Post, - acclaimed author of ‘The Lost World of the Kalahari’ and ‘A Far Off Place’ amongst others. It’s was a house steeped in layers of history and memorabilia, but not many creature comforts.

(Doreen) I must say when we landed up here we said to ourselves what on earth have we done? What have we done, Internet was utterly impossible. There was no TV signal. The only radio reception was in the toilet. So we installed a plug Just so that we could keep our radio plugged in.

(Claire) Philippolis is named after the Reverand Doctor John Philip, from the London Missionary Society. It was John Philip, who invited Griqua leader, Adam Kok with his people to come and settle in Philippolis

(Doreen) Griqua were Dutch speaking, they were mixed race. They were modern. They rode horses. They had excellent, firearms and skills. John Philip understood that we need to prove to the world that black or colored ,democratic, modern republics can flourish. What a far sighted view. And that dream lasted for about 20 years, and then it got overtaken by history. So we are honored to have his name in our town.

(Claire) What a wonderful legacy.

(Claire) Morning Good morning why didn’t you tell me it was so cold in this place…

(Hanneke) I think, without realizing it, really, I was looking for a bigger canvas. Jo'burg was fantastic, but, there was something that always felt kind of amiss that I needed to listen to my own voice a little bit more.

(Claire) It was the onset of Covid that was the final push that brought Hanneke Bentz and her husband Kevin to the dorp.

(Hanneke) We packed our bags one afternoon in Jo'burg as lockdown was happening, because we thought it would be for three weeks and we never, came, we never went back.

(Claire) And they haven’t let the Karoo veld grow under their feet. Initially buying the guesthouse, Dusty Vine; then a few years later Emily’s restaurant. Her latest project is a vegetable patch at the local school, Bergmanshoogte.

(Hanneke) I think that's another important thing. If you do move to a small town, you have to become part of the community. We started with the kids, with the little tykes they all got stuck in and we started preparing the land and started planting things and the season was generous and the kids seem to enjoy it and It’s wonderful to see the food ending up right in the kitchen.

(Claire) Where it’s needed the most.

(Hanneke) I'm someone with a very busy mind, and, this place grounds me and brings me peace. Like I haven't found anywhere else.

(Claire) On the shelves of the Karoo Café are bottles of ‘Made in Philippolis’ mead.

(Claire) I like it okay

(Claire) It’s an ancient beverage older than wine and beer.

(Neil) So mead, by definition, is fermented honey and water.

(Claire) Neil Underhuy is the brewer. And he makes mead the traditional way from his bees, from the honeycomb and the hives

(Neil) You’re going to need another batch just to get it up there.

(Claire) Neil, with his three children Matilda, Alexander and Noah, moved from Johannesburg, to this small holding. just outside Philippolis, a year and a half ago. The goal was a more environmental lifestyle.

(Claire)Moving your family

(Neil) Yeah

(Claire) Understanding what that upheaval would mean? What was the thing,?
(Neil) The core was always there to be outside of the city. It is off grid. You don’t have a choice. You have to be, self-reliable, self-sustainable here. After Covid, as weeks came by, and the opportunity to become more real it was like okay this can happen.

(Claire ) And in the process, Neil -a bespoke furniture maker- became passionate about bees. It started with a visit to a bee keeper.

(Neil) I just fell in love with the smell of it and the idea of it and the more I spoke to him the more it fascinated me.

(Claire) And now you’re the only bee keeper in the area.

(Neil) Well Ya

(Claire)This is a completely new way of life for Neil and his family. Matilda is at boarding school, the boys are being home schooled on line.

(Claire) What has that been like for kids moving to ..

(Neil) To here? I think it was, for the most part, exciting. It was also challenging. It’s a Roller coaster because you don't know what you're in for. And they've been a huge inspiration, because they see things differently.

(Claire) If the measure of a dorp is it’s church then Philippolis stands proud. The church was used as a fort by the British when they occupied the town in the Second Boer War in 1900

(Doreen) So the British settled here, and things quietened down and the war went up towards Johannesburg and Pretoria. However after the fall of Pretoria, people like General de Wet and General Hertzog said No no no things are way too quiet in the South let’s go wake them up.

(Claire) October 1900 ,the Boers made their successful assault on Philippolis.

(Doreen) The Boers attacked from the East, over that mountain, came in this side, this was pretty much the edge of the town.

(Claire) Doreen’s back garden was the site of these Boer battles… and to this day she finds old cartridges, remnants of those battles.

(Claire) With raids by the Boer Commando’s and counter attacks by the British forces this town was a hot bed of unrest and intrigue A time when this jail was put to good use but today there are occupants of a different kind…..

(Claire) Visitors to Philippolis can have the somewhat dubious pleasure of a night spent locked up. Or is it, I’m a celebrity, Get Me Out of here.

(Claire) So is there where people are supposed to throw eggs and rotten tomatoes at me
(Claire) In this rather eclectic community there are connections everywhere, like this organ in the church it brought the community together over a hundred years ago and it continues to do so even today.

(Nicolene) The organ also has got a lovely history so we’re very close to our Jewish community here and always have been. Straight after the Boer war the church was trashed, the organ was trashed and people were really downhearted…

(Claire) It was the Jewish Community, the Boere – Jode who raised the money for a new organ. Built in England it was shipped to Cape Town Harbour.

(Nicolene) We're talking 1905, 1906. So probably ox wagons or something. Just imagine, like this beautiful instrument just in pieces, just making its way up to little old Philippolis. And then it was assembled here.

(Claire) Wow.

(Nicolene) And it used to be just driven by bellows. It's only later that electricity was added

(Claire) Pianist, composer and lecturer Nicolene Gibbons spent 30 years in the UK pursuing her craft.

(Nicolene) And then I decided I wanted to come back. Mostly I missed the sunshine. And it's literally a finger on a map. And I thought, oh, I like the name Philippolis, but something just drew me.

(Claire) You had never been here before?

(Nicolene) I haven't, no.. But when I drove into Philippolis, the energy was just, oh, this is it. This is the right place.

(Claire) Her weeks are spent in Bloemfontein teaching music at the University of the Free State, weekends she’s back in Philippolis, it’s an hours or so drive … When the church organist passed away, the community came looking.

(Nicolene) I was asked to step in. And I'm not an organist at all, but there's such, a dearth of organists in the countryside. So I taught myself.

(Nicolene) I improvise everything, I've got no music.

(Nicolene) What's interesting here in this community is that the people almost they see the organ as their organ. So, you know, they’re championing this instrument and it's almost like another character in the Dorp.

(Claire) Her weeks are spent in Bloemfontein teaching music at the University of the Free State, weekends she’s back in Philippolis, it’s an hours or so drive … When the church organist passed away, the community came looking. (Nicolene) I was asked to step in. And I'm not an organist at all, but there's such, a dearth of organists in the countryside. So I taught myself. (Nicolene) I improvise everything, I've got no music. (Nicolene) What's interesting here in this community is that the people almost they see the organ as their organ. So, you know, they’re championing this instrument and it's almost like another character in the Dorp.

metadata.Summary: In the 1960's the great Karoo through road was built, the N1 highway establishing what was to become a popular road trip between Johannesburg and Cape Town. But the highway bypassed the small town of Philippolis and there was great sadness amongst its residents. No tourist trap, no motels, or immediate job bonanza for the locals. The three petrol stations that the town boasted dwindled to one. Buildings and farms were abandoned as residents left for more lucrative locations. But the N1 omission has turned out to be a blessing in disguise. This little southern Free State dorp tucked away off the N1 at the toe of the Horizon Route has the idyllic atmosphere you would expect of a Karoo town and has retained its old world charm mingled with an air of benevolent neglect. The London Missionary Society founded Philippolis in 1823 as a mission station to serve the local Griquas. This makes it the oldest settlement town in the Free State at over 200 years. Philippolis has retained most of its Karoo architecture. Wide streets, slope-roofed homes, the Dutch Reformed Church (which centres the town) has an imposing organ gifted by the Jewish Community (more of this later) to the Boers after the Anglo Boer War.
metadata.Further information: Nicolene Gibbons, an international pianist (of some repute) bought a small 32 square metre place in the town and while she lectures at Free State University in the week, on the weekends she's in 'Philly' playing the organ at Sunday's church service. This was the home of Sir Laurens van der Post ( his ashes are in the Memorial Garden and the museum has some of his original works) and Griqua leader Adam Kok. Human rights activist Emily Hobhouse established a weaving and spinning school in 1905 for the destitute. More contemporary, this is Brumilda Van Rensburg's home town and Banyana Banyana striker Nthabiseng Majiya ( remarkable that she made the team if you see the condition of the local soccer field) The town played a central role in the Anglo Boer war. Captured by the British, Philippolis came under siege in 1900 during the Boer Commando's struggle to liberate it. Raids and skirmishes between the two sides during this time created a huge occupancy of the local jail house. Today the jail has occupants of a different kind, it's been transformed into an overnight stay for tourists. A more traditional way to experience the history is with historian and journalist Doreen Atkinson. Doreen has vivid stories to tell and she is committed to telling the history of the area reaching out to other museums in the area. Meintjies Louw - Head of the Griekwa community in town, will talk about their history and heritage. Being so close to Joburg, Philly has become a popular semigration spot... Hanneke and her husband Kevin (an editor on international documentaries which is slightly problematic with the sometimes shaky internet connections ) moved here from the City of Gold. They bought a vacant lot of land and have planted vines, experimenting with farming on bio dynamic principles and natural fermentation. The first harvest will be next year but this week she has an experimental first 40 litres to taste. Haneke has also restored some of the old homes where tourists can stay. Another new resident with as story to tell is Neil Underhay - Neil moved with his two children a year and a half ago. A carpenter he made bespoke furniture in Joburg. He bought a half acre plot and started bee keeping…bees and the study of bees had become more and more of his passion. Only beekeeper in this area.. He started to make mead…using not just the honey but the honey comb all parts of the hive. Neil has recently become head of the Free State SAMMA (South African Mead Masters Association) chapter. Philippolis has always attracted eccentric and interesting characters like salesman Jacob Novozenitz, from Lithuania, at the turn of the 20th century. Local Boer farmers gave him money to bring out the rest of his family and this was the beginning of the Boere-Jode in the dorp (and the organ which was donated to the NG Kerk in gratitude). Because the Boers could not pronounce Novozenitz, the was known as Jacob 'Jacob' which eventually transformed to Jacobson. 'Queen of the Free State 'and 'The Messiah's Dream Machine' by author Jennifer Friedman (originally Jacobson) are two memoirs of her childhood and her eccentric family – the Jacobsons. The 'dream machine', a series 1 Land Rover, can be found in brothers Wilfred and Benjamin Jacobson's farm. They farm sheep, produce wool. And continue the Jacobson's legacy of eccentricity.
